Goal Zero Crush Light Chroma vs Streamlight Siege Compact: Which Compact Lantern Belongs in Your Kit?

One collapses flat and charges from the sun. The other throws 540 lumens and floats. They look like substitutes — they are almost opposite tools.

Updated November 2026 · Outdoor & Camping · 8 min read

The Quick Take

These two lanterns are the most-recommended "small camp lights" in their price bracket, and almost every review treats them as interchangeable. They are not. The Goal Zero Crush Light Chroma is a rechargeable, solar-topped puck that squashes down to 0.6 inches thick and weighs about as much as a smartphone. The Streamlight Siege Compact is a purpose-built emergency light running three D alkaline cells, throwing 540 lumens, floating in water, and rated to survive being left in a garage for five years.

The honest framing is this: the Goal Zero is a lantern you will actually carry and use every weekend, while the Streamlight is a lantern you buy once and hope to never need — and then need it for 295 straight hours. Choose wrong and you either pack a brick you never use, or you reach for your "daily" light during a storm and find it dead in a drawer.

Our Pick Goal Zero Crush Light Chroma Collapsible Solar Lantern

At $34.95 versus $45.49, the Goal Zero wins on the thing that decides most real purchases: whether the light is on you when you need it. It has a built-in 1.85Wh lithium battery that refills from USB-C in 2.5 hours or from sunlight in about 20, it packs down to a sixth of its lit height, and it costs nothing in batteries forever. The Streamlight is the objectively brighter and tougher tool — but a lantern you leave at home because it doesn't fit the pocket is worth zero lumens.

Brightness: This Is Where the Streamlight Wins Decisively

Let's not sand this off. The Siege Compact puts out 540 lumens against the Goal Zero's 60 — nine times the light. In practice that is the difference between lighting a picnic table and lighting a site. The Streamlight's 360-degree optic with the globe removed will genuinely illuminate a cabin room, a tarp, or the side of a vehicle well enough to work under. The Goal Zero will light a tent, a book, and your immediate table area, and beyond about six feet it stops being a work light.

Measured per dollar, the Streamlight is also the better raw-value buy: roughly 12 lumens per dollar against Goal Zero's under 2. If your single criterion is "how much light do I get for my money," the Siege Compact is not close.

⚡ Reality check: Lumens are only half the story. A 60-lumen diffused 360° lantern in a two-person tent is bright enough to cook dinner by. The excess output of the Streamlight matters at the campsite or the job site, not inside a tent.

Power: USB-C and Solar Versus Three D Cells

This is the comparison that actually decides the award. The Goal Zero has a built-in 1.85Wh lithium-polymer pack: plug it into any USB-C cable and it's full in 2.5 hours, or leave it on a windowsill or dashboard and the integrated panel will refill it in roughly 20 hours of sun. It never buys a battery again.

The Streamlight takes three D alkalines — sold separately. That's a real hidden cost at checkout, and a recurring one. Alkalines also self-discharge and, left installed for a year, are a known leakage risk that can write off the lantern. The upside, and it's a serious one for preppers: a sealed pack of D cells stored alongside the lantern will still be good half a decade from now, whereas a lithium cell sat empty in a drawer for two years is not going to be happy. Runtime is where that pays out — 295 hours on low is over twelve continuous nights of light.

Portability: Not Even Competitors

The Crush Light collapses to 0.6 inches and weighs 3.2 ounces. It disappears into a jacket pocket, a glovebox, a desk drawer, the lid of a backpack. It is the rare lantern you never have to decide to pack, which is precisely why it gets used. Goal Zero designed it to survive being crushed — hence the name — inside a bag of gear.

The Siege Compact is a fixed-bodied, roughly 5-inch lantern whose three D cells add close to a pound before the housing. This is a lantern that lives in a go-bag, a shed, or a emergency kit, not one you toss in a daypack. Nobody calls it bulky; it simply isn't the same class of portable.

Build, Weather, and Where Each One Shines

Streamlight made this for professionals and hurricane country. It's rated to survive a metre of water for thirty minutes, it floats, it has a recessed power button so it can't switch itself on in a pack, spring-loaded D-rings top and bottom so it can hang inverted off a branch or a ladder, and a red SOS mode that runs 430 hours. That is a life-safety spec sheet.

The Goal Zero is not an immersion-rated light. It's a fair-weather, camp-and-cabin lantern that adds something the Streamlight has no answer for: seven colour modes, a multicolour auto-fade, and a candle-flicker setting that runs 3.5 hours. It sounds like a gimmick until you're sitting outside after dark and realise a warm red glow makes a campsite feel like a room and a bare white LED makes it feel like a crime scene.

The Verdict

Buy the Goal Zero Crush Light Chroma if you want a light you'll carry every trip and keep in a drawer for power blips. Rechargeable forever, no battery tax, packs flatter than a paperback, and $10.54 cheaper. It is the better daily lantern for hikers, car campers, RV owners, festival-goers, and anyone who wants colour or candle ambience.

Buy the Streamlight Siege Compact if the lantern's job is to be there when things go badly. Nine times the output, 295 hours on low, floats, survives immersion, hangs anywhere, and will wake up fully capable after five years on a shelf with a spare pack of D cells. For hurricane prep, job sites, power outages with real work to do, and marine use, it's the more trustworthy device — and honestly the better value per lumen on the market.

Our pick, because most people need one light and will actually carry it: the Goal Zero. But if you're building an emergency kit rather than a camping kit, reverse that answer without hesitating.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 60 lumens enough for camping?

Inside a tent or at a single picnic table, yes — a diffused 360° 60-lumen lantern reads far brighter than a bare 60-lumen flashlight. For lighting a whole campsite, navigating a dark campground, or working under a vehicle, no. That's a Streamlight job.

Does the Goal Zero solar panel actually charge it?

Yes, but slowly and honestly: about 20 hours of direct sun for a full refill. Treat solar as a way to top up on a multi-day trip or keep it alive in a window, not as your primary charging method. USB-C is the real answer at 2.5 hours.

Can I make the Streamlight rechargeable?

You can drop in rechargeable D cells, but the Siege Compact 44931 has no charging circuit, so you'd charge them outside the lantern in a separate charger. If built-in rechargeability matters, that's the Goal Zero's territory.

Which is better for power outages?

The Streamlight, clearly. 295 hours on low means a week-long outage barely dents one set of cells, the batteries store for years, and it survives being knocked into a bucket of water. Keep a Goal Zero for convenience; keep a Siege for the event.
